title: Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Statins are widely continued for primary prevention into advanced age, but the safety of deprescribing them in older adults with multimorbidity and no established cardiovascular disease had not been tested in an adequately sized randomized trial. The STREAM trial was presented as late-breaking science at the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 and published simultaneously. METHODS: STREAM was an investigator-initiated, international, multicentre, open-label, randomized non-inferiority trial with blinded adjudication of outcomes, conducted in Switzerland, the Netherlands and France. Participants were adults 70 years of age or older who had at least two chronic conditions, no known cardiovascular disease, and were taking a statin for primary prevention. They were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to discontinue the statin or to continue it. A total of 1880 participants underwent randomization (secondary reports describe the cohort as 'more than 1880' and 'nearly 1900'); enrolment ran from November 2021 to April 2025. The primary outcome was the first occurrence of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause. Non-inferiority was assessed as the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of -5.2 weeks. RESULTS: Restricted mean event-free survival at 2 years was 96.5 weeks in the discontinuation group and 98.5 weeks in the continuation group, a difference of -2.0 weeks (95% CI, -3.7 to -0.3), which lay within the prespecified -5.2-week margin; discontinuation therefore met the criterion for non-inferiority. Over a median follow-up of 103 weeks, a primary-outcome event occurred in 119 participants (12.7%) in the discontinuation group and in 87 participants (9.2%) in the continuation group. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 43.0% of participants assigned to discontinuation and 39.8% of those assigned to continuation. CONCLUSIONS: In older adults with multimorbidity but without cardiovascular disease, discontinuing statin therapy was non-inferior to continuing it with respect to event-free survival at 2 years, and was described by the investigators as generally safe. Because primary-outcome events were nevertheless more frequent in the discontinuation group over longer follow-up, the investigators and the AHA emphasized that deprescribing should be a patient-centred, shared decision rather than a routine step.
omitido: OMITIDO POR FUENTE UNICA (no se pudo confirmar con 2 fuentes independientes): el valor de p de no-inferioridad (una fuente secundaria da P<0.001); el numero exacto de centros (una fuente da 24 centros; los paises Suiza/Paises Bajos/Francia si estan en 2 fuentes mas el protocolo); la edad media (una fuente da 77.5 anos). NO VERIFICADO EN ABSOLUTO: hazard ratio del objetivo primario e IC95% (las fuentes solo dan la diferencia de supervivencia media restringida, no un HR); desglose por componentes (IAM, ictus, muerte) por separado; objetivos secundarios (LDL-C alcanzado, calidad de vida, mortalidad cardiovascular); numero de pacientes por brazo. Nota de contexto: un analisis de opinion (Substack de J. Stein) critica que el margen no escalase con la tasa de eventos del control y que el ensayo se dimensiono para una tasa de eventos del 34% a 2 anos en el grupo control; es opinion no revisada por pares y no se usa como cifra del ensayo.

title: Left Bundle-Branch Pacing versus Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block
abstract: BACKGROUND: Conventional right ventricular pacing produces electrical and mechanical dyssynchrony and can cause pacing-induced cardiomyopathy in patients who require a high ventricular pacing burden. Left bundle-branch pacing is a conduction-system pacing alternative, but randomized outcome data were lacking. OptimPacing was presented as late-breaking science at the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 and published simultaneously. METHODS: OptimPacing was an investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized trial. Patients with atrioventricular block and an indication for permanent pacemaker implantation with an anticipated high ventricular pacing burden were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to left bundle-branch pacing or right ventricular pacing. A total of 702 patients underwent randomization. The primary outcome was a composite of death from any cause, hospitalization for heart failure, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The trial was stopped early, on the recommendation of the independent data monitoring committee, after a planned interim analysis showed that left bundle-branch pacing had crossed the prespecified threshold for superiority. RESULTS: Left bundle-branch pacing significantly reduced the primary composite outcome as compared with right ventricular pacing (hazard ratio, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.23 to 0.75). The 4-year Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence of the primary outcome was 19.2% in the right ventricular pacing group. The AHA described the result as a 59% lower risk of the composite of death, heart failure hospitalization and pacing-induced cardiomyopathy, consistent with that hazard ratio. No patient in the left bundle-branch pacing group developed pacing-induced cardiomyopathy, as compared with 11.7% of patients in the right ventricular pacing group. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with atrioventricular block requiring a high burden of ventricular pacing, left bundle-branch pacing was superior to right ventricular pacing for the composite of death, heart failure hospitalization and pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The investigators concluded that left bundle-branch pacing should be a first-line pacing strategy in this population. Two caveats were raised by the AHA: early termination for benefit may overestimate the treatment effect and widen confidence intervals, and all left bundle-branch procedures used a single lead type, so the findings may not generalize to other pacing hardware.
omitido: OMITIDO POR FUENTE UNICA: el valor de p del objetivo primario (una fuente da log-rank estratificado P=0.003); la asignacion por brazo (una fuente da 348 a marcapasos de rama izquierda y 354 a estimulacion ventricular derecha, con 17 excluidos antes del implante); el numero de eventos primarios (una fuente da 16 frente a 35); la mediana de seguimiento (una fuente da 35.1 meses); la incidencia acumulada a 4 anos en el brazo de rama izquierda (una fuente da 8.5%; el 19.2% del brazo ventricular derecho si esta en 2 fuentes); y las hospitalizaciones por insuficiencia cardiaca (una fuente da 1.5% frente a 2.9%). NO VERIFICADO: numero de centros y paises participantes; criterios de inclusion detallados (FEVI de partida, tipo de bloqueo AV); mortalidad por separado; complicaciones del procedimiento, umbrales y parametros del electrodo; definicion exacta de miocardiopatia inducida por estimulacion. Nota: no confundir con el ensayo distinto de estimulacion de area de rama izquierda con FEVI conservada publicado en JAMA el 28-10-2026, ni con LBBP-FAVOUR (JACC, abril 2026).

title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
ptype: Estudio comparativo no aleatorizado (despliegue escalonado por conglomerados)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is usually started in hospital, which delays cannulation. ON-SCENE tested whether starting extracorporeal life support at the scene, delivered by helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS), improves survival. The results were presented at the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 and published simultaneously. METHODS: ON-SCENE was a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, designed as a stepped deployment in which HEMS stations equipped and trained to deliver prehospital ECPR were compared with HEMS stations not so equipped, which provided conventional care. Eligible patients were young adults (reported as 18 to 50 years of age in the published protocol and as 50 years of age or younger in the trial report) with witnessed refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge. RESULTS: Survival until hospital discharge occurred in 57 of 144 patients (40%) in the group managed by HEMS teams equipped for prehospital ECPR, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional-care group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.59 to 4.66). A favorable neurologic outcome at 6 months was reported in 36% of the prehospital-ECPR group and 13% of the conventional-care group. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating prehospital extracorporeal life support into helicopter emergency medical services was associated with higher survival until hospital discharge. Because the comparison was not randomized, the findings are associations rather than proof of causation, and independent commentators stressed two points: the intervention was a whole package (an ECPR training programme, femoral ultrasound and video consultation with ECMO intensivists), and the study is best read as hypothesis-generating and strong enough to justify a randomized trial.
omitido: OMITIDO POR FUENTE UNICA: el valor de p del objetivo primario (una fuente da P=0.002) y la odds ratio del resultado neurologico favorable a 6 meses (una fuente da OR 4.22; los porcentajes 36% frente a 13% si constan en 2 fuentes). NO VERIFICADO: numero de bases HEMS y de conglomerados en cada grupo; periodo de reclutamiento; tiempos (desde la llamada a la canulacion, duracion de la RCP convencional antes del ECPR); criterios exactos de refractariedad; ritmo inicial; tasa de canulacion lograda y complicaciones de la canulacion; donacion de organos; mortalidad a 30 dias; analisis ajustados. ATENCION DE DISENO: no es un ensayo aleatorizado, por lo que no debe presentarse como tal en la ficha; las cifras disponibles proceden en su mayor parte del resumen del articulo reproducido por fuentes secundarias.

title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest
abstract: BACKGROUND: Survival with a favorable neurologic outcome after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains near 10% in most communities, and it is unclear whether a coordinated community and emergency medical services (EMS) implementation programme can improve it. RACE-CARS (RAndomized Cluster Evaluation of Cardiac ARrest Systems) was presented as late-breaking science at the AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 and published simultaneously. METHODS: RACE-CARS was a registry-based, pragmatic, cluster-randomized trial of adults 18 years of age or older with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest attended by EMS in 60 counties of North Carolina. Counties were grouped into clusters and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to a multifaceted intervention or to usual care. The intervention had four components: training of 911 telecommunicators to improve rapid recognition of cardiac arrest; training of 911 telecommunicators to improve delivery of CPR instructions; community CPR training; and enhanced use of automated external defibrillators before EMS arrival. Outcomes were ascertained through the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES). The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome. A total of 11,615 patients were included in the intervention group and 10,844 in the usual-care group (22,459 patients in all). RESULTS: The multifaceted community and EMS implementation strategy did not result in a greater percentage of patients surviving to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care; the difference between groups was not statistically significant. Bystander CPR was performed in 44.8% of arrests in intervention communities and 42.3% in control communities, and the programme did not improve overall rates of bystander CPR or of bystander defibrillation. CONCLUSIONS: A multifaceted community and EMS implementation strategy did not improve survival with a favorable neurologic outcome after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The investigators noted an apparent improvement in bystander performance in the final year of the trial and suggested that a longer horizon, or mandatory CPR education of the kind used in Denmark, may be needed before a survival benefit becomes measurable.
omitido: CIFRA CLAVE NO VERIFICADA Y POR TANTO OMITIDA DEL ABSTRACT: las tasas del objetivo primario por brazo. Una sola fuente (nota de prensa de la AHA, redistribuida por NewMediaWire, que cuenta como una sola fuente) da aproximadamente 9% en las comunidades de intervencion frente a 9.4% en las de control; no se ha encontrado una segunda fuente independiente que lo confirme, asi que no debe citarse la cifra. OMITIDO POR FUENTE UNICA: el numero de conglomerados por brazo (una fuente da 28 conglomerados de intervencion y 27 de cuidado habitual) y el periodo de estudio (una fuente da julio 2022 a junio 2026). DISCREPANCIA ENTRE FUENTES, NO RESUELTA: la nota de la AHA dice que 31 condados recibieron la intervencion y 29 continuaron su practica habitual (60 condados), mientras el resumen del articulo habla de 28 y 27 conglomerados y el articulo de diseno de 60 condados agrupados en 57 conglomerados; condado y conglomerado no son la misma unidad, pero las cifras no cuadran entre si. La AHA describe un periodo de estudio de cinco anos y el articulo de diseno un ensayo pragmatico de siete anos. NO VERIFICADO: odds ratio o riesgo relativo del objetivo primario con IC95% y p; supervivencia global al alta; tasas de desfibrilacion por testigos con cifras; reconocimiento del paro por el teleoperador; resultados del ultimo ano citados como senal de mejora; definicion operativa del resultado neurologico favorable en el analisis publicado (el articulo de diseno la define como CPC 1-2).

title: 2026 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations
abstract: SCOPE: This is the annual Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR) of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR), the document from which member councils (including the AHA and the ERC) derive their resuscitation guidelines; its audience is therefore guideline developers, resuscitation councils, educators and clinicians who resuscitate. For the 2026 cycle ILCOR evaluated new evidence through 16 systematic reviews, 9 scoping reviews and 21 evidence updates, spanning all of its task forces: Basic Life Support, Advanced Life Support, Pediatric Life Support, Neonatal Life Support, Education, Implementation and Teams, and First Aid. Only systematic reviews can generate a full CoSTR with new or updated treatment recommendations; scoping reviews and evidence updates cover the remaining topics without producing new recommendations. Recommendations are graded with GRADE (strength of recommendation plus certainty of evidence), not with the AHA Class of Recommendation / Level of Evidence system. NEW AND UPDATED RECOMMENDATIONS: The 2026 treatment recommendations are oriented mainly towards CPR quality rather than new therapies, with updates in the areas of ventilation parameters, airway management, defibrillation practices and chest-compression quality. The ventilation-parameters recommendations for adult cardiac arrest, taken verbatim from the ILCOR CoSTR documentation, are: 'We suggest delivering 2 ventilations for every 30 compressions or 10 ventilations per minute (1 every 6 seconds) for continuous compressions in adults with cardiac arrest with or without an advanced airway (Weak recommendation, very low certainty of evidence)'; and 'When tidal volume can be measured, we suggest delivering a tidal volume of 400-600 ml (or 6-10 millilitres per kilogram of ideal/predicted body weight) in adults with cardiac arrest (Weak recommendation, very low certainty of evidence)'. These are accompanied by a good practice statement: 'When providing manual ventilation, it is reasonable to deliver enough volume to produce visible chest rise (Good Practice Statement)'. The supporting adult ventilation systematic review screened 3021 titles and abstracts and identified 11 adult studies for analysis (3 randomized trials and 8 observational studies), pediatric studies having been moved to a separate Pediatric Life Support review. KEY MESSAGES: Most of the new treatment recommendations rest on low or very low certainty of evidence; the document highlights substantial knowledge gaps and the need for large, high-quality randomized trials across many resuscitation topics. ILCOR also refined its methodology for good practice statements in 2026, evaluating the 150 active good practice statements across all task forces (36.2% of all statements) and stating that a good practice statement should be the exception rather than the default route to a treatment recommendation, with treatment recommendations developed primarily as GRADEd recommendations even when based on indirect evidence. The intraosseous versus intravenous drug administration review was updated in January 2026 after one included trial was retracted, leaving two randomized trials; its conclusions did not change. Several drowning topics in Basic Life Support (compression-only CPR in drowning cardiac arrest, immediate resuscitation in the water or on a boat, ABC versus CAB sequencing, ventilation equipment and prehospital oxygen) were handled as evidence updates in this cycle.
omitido: NO HAY CLASES NI NIVELES AHA: ILCOR usa GRADE (recomendacion fuerte/debil + certeza de la evidencia), no Clase I/IIa/IIb/III ni Nivel A/B/C; por eso no se indica ninguna clase ni nivel, y no debe anadirse ninguno en la ficha. NO VERIFICADO: la lista completa de recomendaciones nuevas o modificadas de 2026. Solo se ha podido leer textualmente el bloque de parametros de ventilacion en el adulto (mas su good practice statement). El texto literal de las recomendaciones de manejo de la via aerea, desfibrilacion y calidad de las compresiones NO se ha leido: solo consta, por una unica fuente (resumen de la AHA en Professional Heart Daily), que son las areas actualizadas. OMITIDO POR FUENTE UNICA: la mencion fragmentaria a un nuevo good practice statement sobre carga anticipada del desfibrilador (texto demasiado fragmentado para citarlo). NO VERIFICADO: a que edicion sustituye formalmente este documento (el CoSTR anterior es el de 2025, publicado en un suplemento de Circulation de octubre de 2025, pero no se ha leido ninguna frase que declare la sustitucion); numero exacto de recomendaciones nuevas frente a modificadas; los temas de Pediatric Life Support, Neonatal Life Support, Education/Implementation/Teams y First Aid de este ciclo uno por uno; la lista de autores y task forces. DISCREPANCIA DE VERSIONES: el documento accesible en ilcor.org esta etiquetado como preprint de mayo de 2026, mientras el DOI solicitado corresponde a la version de Circulation; las cifras de alcance (16 revisiones sistematicas, 9 revisiones de alcance, 21 actualizaciones de evidencia) coinciden en ambas fuentes, pero el texto final de Circulation no se ha podido leer (red bloqueada a ahajournals.org).
